In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of signal transduction at central synapses that control the basic homeostatic reflex functions of the NTS.
the mechanisms of glutamatergicsynaptic transmission in the solitary tract nucleus and how these mechanisms are modulated by peptide and lipid signaling molecules.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the control of glutamate release from primary afferents in the solitary tract nucleus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NTS is a major site for integration of multiple signals from the periphery and the brain to regulate multiple homeostatic reflex systems.

ST glutamatergicefferent transmission is modulated by a variety of peptide and lipid-like transmitters that differentially regulate glutamate release at specific subsets of second order NTS afferents.
glutamate transmission is modulated by a wide range of peptides and lipids in a highly specific and selective manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
peptide and lipid signaling mechanisms are critical modulators of NTS glutamatergicsynaptic transmission.

peptides and lipids are important regulators of NTS synaptic transmission and that these signals are critical for normal homeostatic regulation of visceral function and may also be involved in disease pathogenesis.
peptide and lipid transmitters control the excitability of ST neurons and thus the strength of homeostatic reflex output.
The main takeaway from our work is that
presynaptic receptors for a variety of transmitters and lipids are expressed at the central terminal of afferents to the solitary tract nucleus.
presynaptic modulation is a key feature of ST transmission that can be used as a target for therapeutic intervention.
ST afferents are not simply afferents but are highly integrated and regulated by peripheral and central signals.
